images.title: Ada Lovelace
images.caption: Lovelace was in her twenties when she worked on the notes published in 1843. This watercolor puts a face to the person imagining what a programmable machine might do.
images.credit: Possibly Alfred Edward Chalon · Science Museum Group

images.title: A surviving part of the Analytical Engine
images.caption: Look at the stacked gears: a number would have a physical position inside the mechanism. Babbage designed a much larger programmable machine. Only parts were built during his lifetime.
images.note: Science Museum, London. This photograph shows a surviving fragment, not a complete working Analytical Engine.

images.title: Inside Ada’s published program
images.caption: Read down the numbered rows on the left: they specify operations. Read across a row: the columns track values in the machine. Near the bottom, the table calls for a group of operations to repeat. This is an algorithm for calculating Bernoulli numbers, written for the proposed Analytical Engine.
images.credit: Ada Lovelace · scan via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: The diagram was published with Lovelace’s notes on her translation of Menabrea’s article. The complete machine was never built in their lifetimes.

images.title: Alan Turing
images.caption: The person behind the 1936 universal-machine idea. His paper described computation using a tape, symbols, and precise rules. The interactive tape below lets you inspect that model.

images.title: Konrad Zuse
images.caption: Zuse worked on both calculating machines and ways to describe programs. Plankalkül grew out of that practical problem: how could someone express a complicated calculation in an organized form?

images.title: Instructions stored inside a machine
images.caption: The Manchester Baby demonstrated a program stored electronically in memory. Inspect the racks and tubes: even a small stored program required substantial hardware. This machine gives physical context to early machine-level programming.
images.note: Replica at the Science and Industry Museum, Manchester; it is not the original 1948 machine.

images.title: A computer becomes an installation
images.caption: UNIVAC was one of the early machines associated with Short Code. The people and cabinets show the scale of that computing environment. A more convenient way to express calculations mattered when operating the computer was a specialized job.

images.title: The hardware behind scientific computing
images.caption: The first Fortran compiler targeted the IBM 704. Look at the console and surrounding equipment: this is the kind of computing installation that scientists wanted to program with formulas.
images.note: Historical IBM 704 photograph. The photo records the hardware; it does not establish which program was running.

images.title: A line of code you could hold
images.caption: The holes encode characters for the computer to read. The printed text lets a person inspect the line. Programs could become decks of these cards, making their physical order part of the work.

images.title: Writing the program before punching it
images.caption: Zoom into the column headings. The form gives line labels, continuation marks, and statements their own places. A programmer could write instructions here before they were transferred onto cards.
images.note: A historical form from the photographer’s collection; the photograph was taken in 2006.

images.title: John McCarthy
images.caption: McCarthy’s interest in artificial intelligence helped shape Lisp. Working with symbols, expressions, and lists became central to the language. Those choices are visible in the nested list example below.

images.title: Grace Hopper at UNIVAC
images.caption: Hopper is seated at the keyboard, third from the left. She helped advance the idea of expressing work in forms people could read and translating those instructions for a machine. COBOL emerged from a committee effort with important influences from that work.
images.credit: Unknown photographer · Smithsonian Institution, via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: Left to right: Donald Cropper, Kalpathi C. Krishnan, Grace Hopper, Norman Rothberg. This photograph predates COBOL.

images.title: A keyboard, a paper roll, and a connection
images.caption: Find the keyboard, printed-paper area, and tape mechanism. Terminals like this let students send commands to a shared computer and receive printed responses. That helps explain BASIC’s PRINT instruction.
images.note: Museum example of the terminal type, not a documented Dartmouth classroom terminal.

images.title: Niklaus Wirth teaching
images.caption: The designer of Pascal, seen teaching decades after its introduction. Pascal’s emphasis on explicit structure suited the task of helping people learn to organize programs.

images.title: A computer with a screen and a mouse
images.caption: Notice the tall display and mouse beside the keyboard. At Xerox PARC, Smalltalk developed in an environment where people could work directly with visible objects on a screen.

images.title: A Smalltalk-76 screen
images.caption: Inspect the overlapping windows and the magnified pixel-editing area. This view of Smalltalk-76 shows the kind of graphical workspace the Alto era helped develop.
images.note: A later capture of historical software, not a photograph taken in 1976.

images.title: Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie
images.caption: Thompson is on the left and Ritchie on the right. Their work on Unix provided a practical setting for C: an operating system needed code that could handle low-level work and remain manageable.
images.note: The surviving source image is small; enlargement preserves its original level of detail.

images.title: Bjarne Stroustrup
images.caption: Stroustrup brought ideas about organizing programs into C’s systems-programming world. The separate objects in the example below reflect one of the major ideas he wanted programmers to be able to express.

images.title: A NeXT workstation with a place in web history
images.caption: Objective-C became closely associated with NeXT’s software tools. This particular NeXT machine at CERN also served as the first web server. Look for the warning label asking people to keep it switched on.
images.note: This is an example of the NeXT environment. The image does not show Objective-C source code.

images.title: Guido van Rossum
images.caption: Van Rossum began Python with an emphasis on practical programming and readable code. His photograph was taken fifteen years after Python’s first public release.

images.title: Yukihiro “Matz” Matsumoto
images.caption: Ruby’s designer placed a strong emphasis on the programmer’s experience. That priority helps explain the language’s expressive syntax and its consistent use of objects.

images.title: James Gosling
images.caption: Gosling helped create Java at Sun Microsystems. Its virtual-machine approach gave developers a way to distribute programs across systems with compatible Java implementations.

images.title: Brendan Eich
images.caption: Eich created the first version of JavaScript at Netscape in 1995. Its early home was the web browser, where code could respond to a reader’s actions on a page.

images.title: Rasmus Lerdorf
images.caption: PHP began with Lerdorf’s tools for his own website and grew into a language used to generate web pages on servers. The request-and-response example below follows that setting.

images.title: Anders Hejlsberg
images.caption: Hejlsberg led the design of C#. The language grew alongside Microsoft’s .NET platform, providing tools for building applications with classes, types, and a managed runtime.

images.title: Martin Odersky
images.caption: Odersky’s Scala combines object-oriented and functional programming. Its place on the JVM also connects it to the platform used by Java.

images.title: Rob Pike
images.caption: Pike co-designed Go with Robert Griesemer and Ken Thompson. The language’s approach to concurrent tasks grew from the needs of large software systems.
